results.title: Designing Self-Aware AI That Doesn't Replicate Human Bias
results.content: By combining technical innovations with interdisciplinary approaches drawn from philosophy, cognitive science, sociology, and ethics, developers can design AI with forms of self-awareness specifically engineered to identify, mitigate, and potentially overcome biases that human designers might overlook or unconsciously integrate. Through a global perspective examining case studies across healthcare, finance, criminal justice, education, and other domains, this essay explores practical approaches to developing self-aware AI systems that actively counteract bias rather than perpetuate it. These technical approaches, when combined, create systems capable of not just detecting bias but actively improving their own fairness over time—the hallmark of truly self-aware AI. 7. Neuroscience-Inspired Self-Monitoring: Drawing from human metacognition research to develop more sophisticated self-assessment mechanisms in AI systems, potentially enabling more nuanced bias detection. By designing systems with explicit self-monitoring capabilities—the ability to evaluate their own performance across diverse populations, recognize their knowledge boundaries, and adapt to changing contexts—we can potentially create AI that identifies and mitigates biases that human developers might miss.

results.title: Biased by Design? Evaluating Bias and Behavioral ...
results.content: To investigate annotation bias in LLMs, we designed a comparative study involving both real and synthetic hotel review datasets, each annotated by a human expert and three different LLMs. This section outlines the data sources, annotation protocols, and generation procedures used to ensure methodological consistency across models and conditions. Figure 1 presents the research design, showing the two datasets (real-world HRAST and synthetic hotel reviews), their annotation by a human expert and three LLMs (using manual and batch modes), and the evaluation of sentiment, topic, and aspect labels through inter-annotator agreement metrics. In sum, the study identifies and empirically demonstrates three distinct forms of AI bias affecting annotation outcomes: (1) repetition bias, driven by the highly redundant structure of synthetic data; (2) behavior bias, contingent upon both the mode of input processing (manual versus bulk) and the nature of the dataset (real versus synthetic); and (3) neutrality bias, reflecting LLMs’ conservative default toward neutral classifications in sentiment annotation, coupled with notable limitations in aspect-based sentiment analysis, particularly when sentences contain contradictory sentiments directed at different aspects or topics.
